elements.text: Race Condition in XV6 Shared Data

elements.name: TextBox 3
elements.text:
Demonstrating Data Inconsistency & Spinlock Synchronization
in the XV6 Kernel Free-List Allocator

elements.name: TextBox 4
elements.text: Platform: XV6 RISC-V  •  QEMU (2 CPUs)  •  WSL Ubuntu

elements.name: Rectangle 1
elements.text: 1. Problem Statement

elements.name: Rectangle 3
elements.text: Multiple CPUs in XV6 share kernel data structures like the physical memory free list.

elements.name: Rectangle 4
elements.text: Without synchronization, concurrent access causes race conditions.

elements.name: Rectangle 5
elements.text: Two CPUs can read the same free-list head and return the same page to different processes.

elements.name: Rectangle 6
elements.text: This leads to duplicate page ownership — corrupting memory.

elements.name: Rectangle 7
elements.text: Goal: Demonstrate the inconsistency, then fix it using XV6's spinlock.

elements.name: Rectangle 1
elements.text: 2. Introduction — Objectives

elements.name: Rectangle 3
elements.text: Understand race conditions and critical sections in kernel code.

elements.name: Rectangle 4
elements.text: Identify shared kernel data structures (kmem.freelist) in XV6.

elements.name: Rectangle 5
elements.text: Study why mutual exclusion is required for multi-CPU access.

elements.name: Rectangle 6
elements.text: Demonstrate data inconsistency when the lock is absent.

elements.name: Rectangle 7
elements.text: Show how XV6's spinlock prevents inconsistent results.

elements.name: Rectangle 8
elements.text: Based on Case Study 14: Race Condition in XV6 Shared Data.

elements.name: Rectangle 1
elements.text: 2. Introduction — Motivation

elements.name: Rectangle 3
elements.text: Modern CPUs have multiple cores — kernel code runs in true parallelism.

elements.name: Rectangle 4
elements.text: A single corrupted page allocation can crash the entire OS.

elements.name: Rectangle 5
elements.text: Understanding synchronization is essential for OS and systems programming.

elements.name: Rectangle 6
elements.text: XV6 is a small, real OS — ideal for studying these mechanisms.

elements.name: Rectangle 7
elements.text: XV6 runs on QEMU with configurable CPU count, making it perfect for multi-core experiments.

elements.name: Rectangle 1
elements.text: 3. Existing System — Background

elements.name: Rectangle 3
elements.text: XV6 manages free physical memory as a linked list (kmem.freelist).

elements.name: Rectangle 4
elements.text: kalloc() pops the head page; kfree() pushes a freed page back.

elements.name: Rectangle 5
elements.text: A spinlock (kmem.lock) protects all accesses to the free list.

elements.name: TextBox 6
elements.text: Table 1. Shared kernel structures and their locks

elements.name: Table 7
elements.text:
Structure	Lock	Purpose
kmem.freelist	kmem.lock	Physical page free list
ptable.proc[]	ptable.lock	Process table
bcache	bcache.lock	Buffer cache for disk blocks

elements.name: Rectangle 8
elements.text: Source: MIT xv6 RISC-V kernel source code.

elements.name: Rectangle 1
elements.text: 3. Existing System — Drawbacks

elements.name: Rectangle 3
elements.text: Single global lock → CPUs spin-wait under high contention.

elements.name: Rectangle 4
elements.text: If the lock is removed, no mechanism prevents concurrent modification.

elements.name: Rectangle 5
elements.text: The production allocator cannot be safely tested without risking kernel crash.

elements.name: Rectangle 6
elements.text: No built-in diagnostic to detect or report race conditions.

elements.name: Rectangle 7
elements.text: These drawbacks motivate a safe, isolated test module for experimentation.

elements.name: Rectangle 1
elements.text: 4. Proposed Solution

elements.name: Rectangle 3
elements.text: Build a test-only kernel module (racecheck.c) mirroring the free-list pattern.

elements.name: Rectangle 4
elements.text: Create a miniature free list with 3 pages: P0 → P1 → P2.

elements.name: Rectangle 5
elements.text: Run two cases on 2 real QEMU CPUs (harts):

elements.name: Rectangle 6
elements.text: Case 1 (UNLOCKED): Both CPUs pop without lock → shows inconsistency.

elements.name: Rectangle 7
elements.text: Case 2 (SPINLOCK): Both CPUs pop with acquire()/release() → consistent.

elements.name: Rectangle 8
elements.text: Audit function verifies page ownership invariant after each case.

elements.name: Rectangle 9
elements.text: The test module keeps XV6's real allocator intact and safe.

elements.name: Rectangle 1
elements.text: 5. Working Flow — Overview

elements.name: Rectangle 3
elements.text: racetest.c (user)  →  calls raceinit() to reset the test list

elements.name: Rectangle 4
elements.text: fork() × 2         →  creates two child processes (one per CPU)

elements.name: Rectangle 5
elements.text: raceworker(id)      →  each child enters kernel, pops from test list

elements.name: Rectangle 6
elements.text: wait() × 2         →  parent waits for both children to finish

elements.name: Rectangle 7
elements.text: racereport()        →  kernel audits & prints results

elements.name: Rectangle 8
elements.text: Repeat for SPINLOCK case with fresh list

elements.name: Rectangle 9
elements.text: Both cases run automatically when the user types 'racetest' at the XV6 shell.

elements.name: Rectangle 1
elements.text: 5. Working Flow — The Critical Section

elements.name: Rectangle 3
elements.text: The kalloc() function performs a two-step operation on shared data:

elements.name: Rectangle 4
elements.text:
acquire(&kmem.lock);           // Step 1: Acquire the lock
r = kmem.freelist;             // Step 2: Read the head pointer
if (r)
    kmem.freelist = r->next;   // Step 3: Advance the head
release(&kmem.lock);           // Step 4: Release the lock

elements.name: Rectangle 5
elements.text: Step 2 (read) and Step 3 (update) depend on each other.

elements.name: Rectangle 6
elements.text: Step 3 assumes Step 2's value is still current. If another CPU

elements.name: Rectangle 7
elements.text: modifies the head between these steps, the assumption breaks.

elements.name: Rectangle 8
elements.text: Source: kernel/kalloc.c — XV6 production allocator.

elements.name: Rectangle 1
elements.text: 6. Implementation — Unlocked Path (Race Condition)

elements.name: Rectangle 3
elements.text: Both CPUs execute this simultaneously — NO lock protection:

elements.name: Rectangle 4
Rectangle 5
elements.text: Both read P0 before either updates → both return P0 (duplicate!)

elements.name: Rectangle 6
elements.text: Source: kernel/racecheck.c lines 115–124. The rendezvous forces the interleaving.

elements.name: Rectangle 1
elements.text: 6. Implementation — Unlocked Timeline

elements.name: TextBox 3
elements.text: Table 2. CPU interleaving without lock (race condition)

elements.name: Table 4
elements.text:
Step	CPU 0 (Worker 0)	CPU 1 (Worker 1)
T1	READ head → gets P0	READ head → gets P0
T2	SAVE next → P1	SAVE next → P1
T3	— rendezvous —	— rendezvous —
T4	WRITE head = P1	WRITE head = P1
T5	RETURN P0  ✓	RETURN P0  ✗ DUPLICATE

elements.name: Rectangle 5
elements.text: Result: P0 given to BOTH processes. Head = P1. INCONSISTENT.

elements.name: Rectangle 6
elements.text: Figure 1. Timeline of unlocked free-list pop showing duplicate allocation.

elements.name: Rectangle 1
elements.text: 6. Implementation — Spinlock Path (Fix)

elements.name: Rectangle 3
elements.text: XV6's acquire()/release() wraps the entire critical section:

elements.name: Rectangle 4
Rectangle 5
elements.text: First CPU gets P0, second waits → then gets P1. No duplicates.

elements.name: Rectangle 6
elements.text: Source: kernel/racecheck.c lines 126–133. Uses XV6's real spinlock.

elements.name: Rectangle 1
elements.text: 6. Implementation — Spinlock Timeline

elements.name: TextBox 3
elements.text: Table 3. CPU interleaving with spinlock (serialized access)

elements.name: Table 4
elements.text:
Step	CPU 0 (Worker 0)	CPU 1 (Worker 1)
T1	— rendezvous —	— rendezvous —
T2	acquire(lock) ✓ GOT IT	acquire(lock) SPINNING...
T3	READ head → gets P0	(waiting)
T4	WRITE head = P1	(waiting)
T5	release(lock)	acquire(lock) ✓ GOT IT
T6		READ head → gets P1
T7		WRITE head = P2
T8	RETURN P0  ✓	RETURN P1  ✓

elements.name: Rectangle 5
elements.text: Figure 2. Timeline showing how spinlock serializes the critical section.

elements.name: Rectangle 3
elements.text:

# Step 2: Navigate to project

make -j4 DETFLAGS= qemu CPUS=2

elements.text: 6. Implementation — Demo Output

elements.name: Rectangle 3
elements.text:
[xv6 race demo] UNLOCKED free-list pop
  user workers ran on harts 0 and 1
  head values read: P0 and P0
  allocated pages: P0 and P0
  same page returned twice: YES
  free-list head after both pops: P1
  page IDs appearing exactly once: 2 / 3
  invariant: INCONSISTENT
  xv6 check: PASS

[xv6 race demo] SPINLOCK free-list pop
  user workers ran on harts 0 and 1
  allocated pages: P0 and P1
  same page returned twice: NO
  free-list head after both pops: P2
  page IDs appearing exactly once: 3 / 3
  invariant: CONSISTENT
  xv6 check: PASS

XV6 RACE DEMO: PASS (inconsistency reproduced; spinlock fixed it)

elements.text: 7. Results

elements.name: TextBox 3
elements.text: Table 4. Comparison of results — Unlocked vs. Spinlock

elements.name: Table 4
elements.text:
Criteria	Without Lock	With Spinlock
CPU 0 gets	P0	P0
CPU 1 gets	P0 (duplicate!)	P1 (unique)
Free list after	P1 → P2	P2
Duplicate allocation	YES	NO
Pages counted once	2 / 3	3 / 3
Data integrity	INCONSISTENT	CONSISTENT
Real-world impact	Memory corruption	Safe allocation

elements.name: Rectangle 1
elements.text: 8. Conclusion — What We Learnt

elements.name: Rectangle 3
elements.text: A lock must cover the full read-and-update that preserves an invariant.

elements.name: Rectangle 4
elements.text: Without mutual exclusion, two CPUs return the same page — data corruption.

elements.name: Rectangle 5
elements.text: XV6's spinlock (acquire/release) serializes access to the critical section.

elements.name: Rectangle 6
elements.text: The same principle applies to any shared structure: process tables, buffers, caches.

elements.name: Rectangle 7
elements.text: Key learning: synchronization is not optional in multi-CPU kernels.

elements.name: Rectangle 1
elements.text: 8. Conclusion — Future Scope & Applications

elements.name: Rectangle 3
elements.text: Test with more CPUs (4, 8) to study increased contention.

elements.name: Rectangle 4
elements.text: Implement per-CPU free lists to reduce lock contention.

elements.name: Rectangle 5
elements.text: Explore other primitives: mutex, semaphore, reader-writer locks.

elements.name: Rectangle 6
elements.text: Apply to real-world systems: database engines, web servers, RTOS.

elements.name: TextBox 7
elements.text: Table 5. Synchronization in real-world applications

elements.name: Table 8
elements.text:
Application Domain	Shared Resource	Sync Method
Database Systems	Buffer pool / page cache	Latch / mutex
Web Servers	Connection pool	Semaphore
RTOS / Embedded	Shared I/O registers	Spinlock / disable IRQ
